title: Sanity's Edge — Voice BBS (1994-1997)
excerpt: Interactive web recreation of Sanity's Edge, a mental asylum-themed voice BBS that ran in Tampa, FL from 1994-1997. 26,188 calls. 46,610 messages. Built by a father and son.

A voice BBS from 1994. Now preserved on the web.

Tampa, FL -- 813-989-1950

The board re-recorded its prompts over the years. Choose the day you are calling.

The date also decides the Halloween greeting (25-31 October), the Halloween 1996 login sounds, the sysop's welcome for new callers and birthdays. Members on the even/odd-day economic plan are told it is not their day when the day of the month ends in the wrong digit: add ?date=1996-06-02 (even) or ?date=1996-06-01 (odd) to the phone page address.

// THE STORY

Sanity's Edge was a bulletin board you could only reach by telephone. No modem, no screen: you dialed, pressed keys, and listened. It ran from 1994 to March 1997 on a dedicated 286 PC in a house in Tampa, Florida, built by a father and his ten-year-old son.

It started in the garage. In a box of odds and ends Max found an open retail box for the BigMouth voice card and its SDK: the card, the SDK software, paper manuals and all. He had already taught himself BASIC, so a development kit caught his eye and he asked his dad about it. “Well, son, let me tell you about SDKs...” was how he learned what one was. Around the same time he got his first computer, an 8086 with no math coprocessor, and his father taught him C on it with Turbo C: how to look up what a function does in the reference manuals, then arrays and tables in more than one dimension.

His father was a radio-station automation programmer who worked from home. He became the sysop, Dr. Null, and wrote the database backend. Max wrote a lot of the rest, including the menu structures, and was a user of the board and its co-creator: the asylum theme was his idea, and he coded the maze himself. He was user number 7, and went by Xela (Alex backwards).

The phone number, 813-989-1950, was Max's own line in his bedroom, wired up for the board; the house had three or four lines because Dad worked from home. Max designed business cards and a full-page flyer and handed them out. Anyone was welcome to call and register. Members paid a monthly fee, about five dollars as Max remembers it, and he opened the envelopes that arrived in the mail.

Callers were admitted to an asylum. Message bases were therapy rooms, the public forums were the “Men in White Jackets,” and every voice left behind became part of the fiction. Over three years the line took more than 26,000 calls and collected more than 46,000 voice messages from friends, schoolmates and strangers around the Tampa Bay area. His mother's voice is on quite a few of the recordings, including “What is Sanity's Edge?”, and his father's younger voice welcomes you to the Men in White Jackets.

Max's father passed away some years ago. Among his hoarded technology and data was a backup of Sanity's Edge, copied from hard disk to hard disk, then to solid state, and finally onto a CD labeled “Sanity's Edge” that Max's mother found and handed to him.

It took three generations of AI, and the Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) project, to crack it. ChatGPT 3, more than a year ago, did a poor job. Sonnet 4 almost cracked everything and built the first museum page, but that page was a bad recreation and the audio never played right. Then Claude Sonnet 5.5 with REA opened it completely: the audio codec turned up in Talking Technology's own converter inside the archive, the program and its logs were read directly, and every recording now plays as it did. The C source that was missing has since been rebuilt, function by function, from the machine code. Read how the code was cracked →

It was a shared creation, and now it has a chance to last. Thank you, Dad, and thank you AI.

The business card belongs on this page too. Photo coming.

// THE ORIGINAL FLYER

What a new caller got in the 1990s: the information sheet (what the board is, the $8 a month plan, who Dr. Null is) and the hand-drawn map of every menu behind the phone. Photographed from the surviving paper copies. Click either one to read it at full size.

Names follow a privacy rule: full names only for callers known to be adults; everyone else is a first name and initial. Private mail is not public. Try the board: Speedo-Man! -- use passcode 616241; Alex Kid -- use passcode 139194; Shenen Rose -- use passcode 172855; Mistique -- use passcode 271653. Called in the 1990s and cannot remember your passcode? Request your mailbox.

// THE TECHNOLOGY

The system ran on a dedicated 286 PC -- modest even by 1994 standards -- equipped with a Talking Technology Powerline I ISA telephony card. This card handled the phone line: answering calls, playing audio prompts, recording voice messages, and reading touchtone key presses.

The software was BigmOuth, a voice BBS platform that turned the PC into a single-line interactive phone system. Callers navigated menus by pressing keys on their phone. There was no text, no screen -- only voice. The entire experience happened through the telephone handset.

Audio was stored in a proprietary format on the hard drive. In February 2026, these files were first decoded into standard WAV format, making it possible to hear the original recordings for the first time in decades.

26,188calls answered

46,610messages recorded

3years online, 1994-1997

The line is open.
